**Coloma** (Nisenan: _Cullumah_, meaning "beautiful") is a census-designated place (CDP)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-6) in El Dorado County, California, United States. It is approximately 36 miles (58 km) northeast of Sacramento. Coloma is most noted for being the site where James W. Marshall found gold in the Sierra Nevada foothills, at [Sutter's Mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutter's_Mill "Sutter's Mill") on January 24, 1848,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-nrhpinv2-3) leading to the California gold rush. As of the 2020 census, Coloma had a population of 521.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-Census2020PLLede-7)
The settlement is a tourist attraction known for its ghost town and the centerpiece of the Marshall Gold Discovery State Historic Park. Coloma was designated a National Historic Landmark District on July 4, 1961.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-nrhpinv2-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-nhlsum-5)
Coloma lies at an elevation of 764 feet (233 m).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-gnis-2)

The name comes from the Nisenan Native Americans name for the valley in which Coloma is located: _Cullumah_, meaning 'beautiful.' Coloma is on the South Fork American River that runs through the valley and was built on the original Indian village of Koloma.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-8) Former spellings include "Colluma" and "Culloma".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-CGN-9)
Coloma grew around Sutter's Mill following the finding of gold. A post office was established in 1849 under the name Culloma, changing to Coloma in 1851.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-CGN-9)
One of Coloma's earliest settlers was Silas Sanderson (1824–1886), who went on to become the 7th Chief Justice of California.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-10) Another was Nancy Gooch, who was one of the first black women to succeed in California.
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ROBERT_BELL'S_STORE,_COLOMA,_CALIFORNIA.jpg)
Robert Bell's store in Coloma
While some people still live in the area, Coloma is considered something of a ghost town because civic buildings such as the jail have been abandoned and left to decay, and other buildings from its boom era (1847–1852) have been converted into museums and other historical displays. The tailrace of Sutter's Mill remains, as does a nearby reconstruction.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-marshall-11)
In reality the meaningfulness of the township of Coloma has dissipated as residents who live in the wider Coloma Valley area generally share a community spirit.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-12)

The local economy is based predominantly on agriculture[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-13) and tourism. Of particular note is the rafting industry as the South Fork American River is one of the most popular white-water trips in North America.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-14)

##### _**The roads were so wretched that supplies could only get to the mines by pack animals. A dollar per pound was the customary rate to Coloma and Hangtown, about the same distance from Sacramento.**_


##### _**Gold dust was the universal currency, and the “blower” and the scales were a fixture in every place of business. The weights were often home-made and of very dubious specific gravity.”**_


##### **— David Leeper, 1849**
Coloma, California in 1857.
Settled along the banks of the South Fork River between Sutter’s Mill and Mormon Island is Coloma, California — the first important mining town of the 1848 gold rush days. Here, on the South Fork River,James Marshallfirst found the gold that started the greatCalifornia Gold Rush. News spread quickly, and by the time it reached San Francisco, thousands began to flood the area.
James Marshall was a construction foreman forJohann (John) Augustus Sutter, who operated Sutter’s Mill on the banks of the American River. Sutter had come to California from his native Switzerland in 1834. By 1839, he had settled in the heart of the Sacramento Valley, where he wanted to establish a “great colony.”
Sutter’s Mill in Coloma, California, by Kathy Alexander.
He began to “build” his colony when Governor Alvarado, the Mexican governor of California, granted him 50,000 acres of prime land. He then purchased several properties that were moved to the area and began raising a herd of cattle. Calling his new colony “New Helvetica,” he used Indian labor to build a “fort,” from which he oversaw his new settlement.
However, he was severely in need of lumber for his buildings. In 1845, he contracted with James Marshall to build a Coloma Valley sawmill about 40 miles east of New Helvetia and Sutter’s Fort. However, it would be two more years before construction on the sawmill would begin. In January 1848, when the mill was nearing completion, Marshall was inspecting the water flow when he discovered a pea-sized gold nugget. Gold had been discovered in California! Ironically, neither Sutter nor Marshall ever profited from the discovery that should have made them independently wealthy.

As word quickly spread, Sutter’s sawmill was overrun by gold miners, around which a gold camp was born. Named for the valley in which it was situated, called Cullumah, meaning “beautiful” to the native Nisenan Indians, the new “town” was called Coloma.
By the summer of 1848, some 80,000 miners had flooded the area, spreading up and down the length of theSacramento Valley, overrunning Sutter’s domain, and trampling his visions of grandeur. Also displaced were the native Nisenan Indianswho had called the Cullumah Valley home for centuries.
In the meantime, the new town of Coloma was booming, already boasting about 300 frame buildings, and a large hotel was under construction. It was the first place fortune-seekers headed when they arrived in San Francisco until gold was discovered in surrounding areas.
By 1849, when the California Gold Rush was in full force, Coloma had several stores, hotels, businesses, and a number of the ever-popularsaloons and gambling houses. But those many new area residents would be shocked to see the outrageous prices. Due to its remote location and the “supply and demand rules,” miners could expect to pay as much as $50 for a pick or shovel.
During Coloma’s mining heydays, the Sierra Nevada Hotel was a way station for miners and tradesmen. Today, it houses an Inn and Restaurant.
The following year, El Dorado County was created in February, and Coloma became its first county seat. Just seven months later, California would become the 31st state. That same year, a six-mile “ditch” was completed to bring water to Coloma from the snowmelt and rain in the mountains so miners could work placers.
When Coloma became the county seat, Captain Shannon, who had built and operated one of Coloma’s first general stores, became the town’s first mayor. Coloma, California in 1857.
Settled along the banks of the South Fork River between Sutter’s Mill and Mormon Island is Coloma, California — the first important mining town of the 1848 gold rush days. Here, on the South Fork River,James Marshallfirst found the gold that started the greatCalifornia Gold Rush. News spread quickly, and by the time it reached San Francisco, thousands began to flood the area.
James Marshall was a construction foreman forJohann (John) Augustus Sutter, who operated Sutter’s Mill on the banks of the American River. Sutter had come to California from his native Switzerland in 1834. By 1839, he had settled in the heart of the Sacramento Valley, where he wanted to establish a “great colony.”
Sutter’s Mill in Coloma, California, by Kathy Alexander.
He began to “build” his colony when Governor Alvarado, the Mexican governor of California, granted him 50,000 acres of prime land. He then purchased several properties that were moved to the area and began raising a herd of cattle. Calling his new colony “New Helvetica,” he used Indian labor to build a “fort,” from which he oversaw his new settlement.
However, he was severely in need of lumber for his buildings. In 1845, he contracted with James Marshall to build a Coloma Valley sawmill about 40 miles east of New Helvetia and Sutter’s Fort. However, it would be two more years before construction on the sawmill would begin. In January 1848, when the mill was nearing completion, Marshall was inspecting the water flow when he discovered a pea-sized gold nugget. Gold had been discovered in California! Ironically, neither Sutter nor Marshall ever profited from the discovery that should have made them independently wealthy.

**Coloma** (Nisenan: _Cullumah_, meaning "beautiful") is a census-designated place (CDP)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-6) in El Dorado County, California, United States. It is approximately 36 miles (58 km) northeast of Sacramento. Coloma is most noted for being the site where James W. Marshall found gold in the Sierra Nevada foothills, at [Sutter's Mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutter's_Mill "Sutter's Mill") on January 24, 1848,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-nrhpinv2-3) leading to the California gold rush. As of the 2020 census, Coloma had a population of 521.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-Census2020PLLede-7)
The settlement is a tourist attraction known for its ghost town and the centerpiece of the Marshall Gold Discovery State Historic Park. Coloma was designated a National Historic Landmark District on July 4, 1961.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-nrhpinv2-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-nhlsum-5)
Coloma lies at an elevation of 764 feet (233 m).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-gnis-2)

The name comes from the Nisenan Native Americans name for the valley in which Coloma is located: _Cullumah_, meaning 'beautiful.' Coloma is on the South Fork American River that runs through the valley and was built on the original Indian village of Koloma.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-8) Former spellings include "Colluma" and "Culloma".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-CGN-9)
Coloma grew around Sutter's Mill following the finding of gold. A post office was established in 1849 under the name Culloma, changing to Coloma in 1851.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-CGN-9)
One of Coloma's earliest settlers was Silas Sanderson (1824–1886), who went on to become the 7th Chief Justice of California.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-10) Another was Nancy Gooch, who was one of the first black women to succeed in California.
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ROBERT_BELL'S_STORE,_COLOMA,_CALIFORNIA.jpg)
Robert Bell's store in Coloma
While some people still live in the area, Coloma is considered something of a ghost town because civic buildings such as the jail have been abandoned and left to decay, and other buildings from its boom era (1847–1852) have been converted into museums and other historical displays. The tailrace of Sutter's Mill remains, as does a nearby reconstruction.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-marshall-11)
In reality the meaningfulness of the township of Coloma has dissipated as residents who live in the wider Coloma Valley area generally share a community spirit.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-12)

The local economy is based predominantly on agriculture[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-13) and tourism. Of particular note is the rafting industry as the South Fork American River is one of the most popular white-water trips in North America.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloma,_California#cite_note-14)

Coloma, California in 1857.
Settled along the banks of the South Fork River between Sutter’s Mill and Mormon Island is Coloma, California — the first important mining town of the 1848 gold rush days. Here, on the South Fork River,James Marshallfirst found the gold that started the greatCalifornia Gold Rush. News spread quickly, and by the time it reached San Francisco, thousands began to flood the area.
James Marshall was a construction foreman forJohann (John) Augustus Sutter, who operated Sutter’s Mill on the banks of the American River. Sutter had come to California from his native Switzerland in 1834. By 1839, he had settled in the heart of the Sacramento Valley, where he wanted to establish a “great colony.”
Sutter’s Mill in Coloma, California, by Kathy Alexander.
He began to “build” his colony when Governor Alvarado, the Mexican governor of California, granted him 50,000 acres of prime land. He then purchased several properties that were moved to the area and began raising a herd of cattle. Calling his new colony “New Helvetica,” he used Indian labor to build a “fort,” from which he oversaw his new settlement.
However, he was severely in need of lumber for his buildings. In 1845, he contracted with James Marshall to build a Coloma Valley sawmill about 40 miles east of New Helvetia and Sutter’s Fort. However, it would be two more years before construction on the sawmill would begin. In January 1848, when the mill was nearing completion, Marshall was inspecting the water flow when he discovered a pea-sized gold nugget. Gold had been discovered in California! Ironically, neither Sutter nor Marshall ever profited from the discovery that should have made them independently wealthy.

As word quickly spread, Sutter’s sawmill was overrun by gold miners, around which a gold camp was born. Named for the valley in which it was situated, called Cullumah, meaning “beautiful” to the native Nisenan Indians, the new “town” was called Coloma.
By the summer of 1848, some 80,000 miners had flooded the area, spreading up and down the length of theSacramento Valley, overrunning Sutter’s domain, and trampling his visions of grandeur. Also displaced were the native Nisenan Indianswho had called the Cullumah Valley home for centuries.
In the meantime, the new town of Coloma was booming, already boasting about 300 frame buildings, and a large hotel was under construction. It was the first place fortune-seekers headed when they arrived in San Francisco until gold was discovered in surrounding areas.
By 1849, when the California Gold Rush was in full force, Coloma had several stores, hotels, businesses, and a number of the ever-popularsaloons and gambling houses. But those many new area residents would be shocked to see the outrageous prices. Due to its remote location and the “supply and demand rules,” miners could expect to pay as much as $50 for a pick or shovel.
During Coloma’s mining heydays, the Sierra Nevada Hotel was a way station for miners and tradesmen. Today, it houses an Inn and Restaurant.
The following year, El Dorado County was created in February, and Coloma became its first county seat. Just seven months later, California would become the 31st state. That same year, a six-mile “ditch” was completed to bring water to Coloma from the snowmelt and rain in the mountains so miners could work placers.
When Coloma became the county seat, Captain Shannon, who had built and operated one of Coloma’s first general stores, became the town’s first mayor. A well-liked and respected man, Shannon was also considered the “official” to settle disputes and punish transgressions. With no official law or judicial system, Shannon complied, often sentencing offenders to banishment, whipping, branding, cutting off one or both ears, and in a few cases – hanging.

Jerry Crane was the first to be hanged in Coloma after murdering one of his students because, as he claimed, he “loved” her. He was later found to have a wife and family back East.
The next man hanged was an outlaw named Mickey Free, who was involved in a cutthroat gang that specialized in raiding and robbing Chinese camps and murdering lonely miners.
But, like other gold-rich boom camps, Coloma’s hectic days were numbered. As the thousands of miners spread out in the area, richer gold veins were soon found at places such as nearby Placerville, Georgetown, Diamond Springs, and as many as 30 other gold camps.
As Coloma’s population began to fall, nearby Placerville, some ten miles away, had become the new “hub” of the Mother Lode, and in 1854, the county seat was moved there, where it remains to this day.
By 1870, Coloma had but just 200 residents and, over the years, continued to dwindle.
